info.description:
SAMM public REST API — everything the admin portal does, scriptable.

## Authentication

Create a token in the admin portal (**System → API**, superadmin only) and send it
on every request:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer samm_YOUR_TOKEN" https://your-samm/api/v1/me
```

The secret is shown **once** at creation; only its SHA-256 hash is stored. A token
carries **scopes** — per-resource grants such as `customers:read` / `customers:write`;
a `write` scope automatically includes the matching `read`. `GET /me` shows the
calling token's effective scopes. Revoking a token makes its calls fail immediately.

## Rate limits

Each token has its own per-minute limit (default 120, set at creation). Exceeding it
returns `429` with `Retry-After` and `X-RateLimit-Limit` / `X-RateLimit-Remaining`
headers — back off and retry.

## Conventions

* List endpoints accept `limit` / `offset` and return `{"total": n, "items": [...]}`.
* Errors: `401` missing/invalid/expired/revoked token · `403` token lacks the required
  scope · `404` not found · `409` duplicate · `422` validation error · `429` rate limit.
* All timestamps are ISO-8601 UTC; all byte counters are plain integers.

## Queued commands

Mutations that touch live accounting state (limit resets, card/group enable/disable,
validity extensions) are **not applied inside the request** — they are queued into the
audited command queue and applied by the `samm-radius` service within one tick
(a few seconds), exactly like the same clicks in the admin portal. These endpoints
reply `{"queued": true}`; poll `GET /commands` to watch your token's commands flip
to `applied`. Everything else (create/update/suspend/renew/pay …) is applied
immediately, and any needed router push (CoA) is queued automatically.

## Webhooks

Register an endpoint (`POST /webhooks` or the admin page) and pick events. Every
delivery carries `X-SAMM-Event` and `X-SAMM-Signature: sha256=<hex>` — the HMAC-SHA256
of the **raw body** with your endpoint's signing secret (returned once at creation):

```python
import hmac, hashlib

def verify(body: bytes, signature_header: str, secret: str) -> bool:
    calc = "sha256=" + hmac.new(secret.encode(), body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return hmac.compare_digest(calc, signature_header)
```

`GET /webhooks/events` lists every event name and what it means — read it rather
than hard-coding the list, since subscribing to a name that does not exist creates
an endpoint that simply never fires. Among them, `alert.opened` / `alert.resolved`
carry the Alert Center's own transitions (router down, service down, rogue DHCP, a
new crash), already deduplicated by the alert engine, so a flapping link sends one
event rather than hundreds.

Failed deliveries retry with exponential backoff; an endpoint that keeps failing is
disabled automatically (re-enable with `POST /webhooks/{id}/enable`, or trial-run
with `POST /webhooks/{id}/test`).

## Two shapes of "expired"

A user is expired either because `status` says so, or because their
expiration limit is exhausted and they were **parked** on a next plan — still
authenticating, against a plan that gives them nothing. `GET /customers?status=expired`
and `/stats/overview` count both, exactly as the admin panel does. Filtering the
raw status field yourself will miss the second group, which is the group that has
already been cut off.

Server version: **5.2.4**

Feed `id` to `GET /customers?assigned_admin_id=` (or pass the username to
`?assigned_admin=`). `customer_count` is the number that lets an operator
confirm they picked the right person before acting on them — "Ali, the one
with 456" is checkable in a way a bare id is not.

`orphaned_customers` counts users whose `assigned_admin_id` points at
an admin row that no longer exists. samm.user.assigned_admin_id carries no
foreign key, so deleting an admin silently strands their users; they
appear under no admin at all and are invisible to every per-admin filter.

get.description:
Search the audit trail. Scope: `logs:read`.

Every filter is optional and they AND together, so "everything that touched
user 412 this week" is one call:

    /api/v1/audit?entity_type=user&entity_id=412&since=2026-08-01

`before`/`after` hold the changed fields and are omitted unless
`include_payload=true`, because they dominate the response and support
usually wants the shape of what happened first, then one row in detail.

delete.description:
Delete an invoice and leave the books consistent. Scope: `billing:write`.

Added because the API could create, pay and reopen an invoice but never
remove one — so an operator whose auto-renew sweep raised 675 invoices by
mistake had no way to undo it programmatically and had to be walked through
the panel.

This is NOT a raw delete. It routes through the accounting service, which:
  * voids the journal entries when nothing was ever collected,
  * writes the remainder off to Bad Debt when the invoice was part paid, so
    the cash and revenue already recognised are preserved,
  * skips the ledger entirely for an agent's off-ledger retail invoice.

Deleting the row without that leaves the receivable alive and attached to
nothing — money the company believes it is owed by no one.

/diagnostics answers "is the machine healthy"; this answers the question
that follows it — "and has the install been TELLING anyone it isn't". They
are not the same: an alert can be open for two days with a healthy snapshot
right now, and a bell nobody has clicked is the most common reason a
user says nothing warned them.

Default is everything unresolved (pending + open + acknowledged), newest
first, because that is the triage question. Pass `status=resolved` for what
cleared. Rides `diagnostics:read`: subjects name a router or a service, not
a user, so this is health data — nothing here needs the separate
consent that tracebacks and daemon logs do.

get.description:
The nightly backup's own record, plus what is actually on disk.

A scheduled backup that has been failing silently is only discovered when
someone needs it. `_backup_auto_last_error` is written every time the sweep
fails and read by nobody; this puts it where support can see it without a
shell, next to the files it claims to have written.

Since SAMM has no update rollback, a current backup is the only floor under
a bad update — so "is this install backed up" is a release question, not
just a support one. Scope: `diagnostics:read`.

get.description:
The pool, the server, and what is holding either of them.

This exists because of one incident shape that reaches us repeatedly: the
panel starts timing out and the captured traceback says
`QueuePool limit of size N overflow M reached` — SQLAlchemy could not get a
connection. That single line cannot distinguish a leak in SAMM from a
Postgres that is refusing connections from a long query holding a lock, and
the difference decides the fix. All three are here.

`pg_stat_activity` shows the query text of OUR OWN backends only (SAMM
connects as one unprivileged role), which is the set that matters; other
roles appear as a state with no text. Query text is masked anyway. Scope:
`diagnostics:read`.
get.summary: PostgreSQL health and the connection pool

get.description:
Incidents from samm.error_report, newest first — deduplicated by
fingerprint with an occurrence count, so a crash loop is ONE row saying
"×4,000" rather than four thousand rows. The traceback is omitted here (it is
long and this is the triage list); fetch one incident for it.

`reported` tells you whether the operator already flagged it for upload, and
`sent` whether it reached SecuryTik — useful when a user says "I sent
you the error" and nothing arrived. Scope: `errors:read`.

`license_last_error` is the whole answer to "it says unlicensed" — a DNS
block on license-samm.securytik.com, a clock so far out that the token
fails validation, a device id that was re-linked elsewhere. The counts are
what the licence is measured against, so an over-limit install shows up
here rather than in a support round trip.

Every `license_*` setting is included EXCEPT the tokens: `_redact()` masks
any key that looks like a credential, which covers `license_token` and
`license_device_token`. Scope: `diagnostics:read`.

get.description:
A bounded tail of one SAMM unit, newest last, with secret shapes masked.

Deliberately narrow: a fixed unit allow-list, at most 1000 lines, at most a
day back. Daemon output can quote usernames and addresses, which is why this
has its own scope instead of riding on `diagnostics:read` — a user grants
log access as a separate, conscious decision. Scope: `logs:read`.

`file=radius.log` reads FreeRADIUS's own log instead of the journal, and it
is not a convenience. FreeRADIUS logs to `${logdir}/radius.log`, so its
startup failures never reach journald: the journal shows only the
`ExecStartPre` config check saying "Configuration appears to be OK" followed
by a bare `status=1/FAILURE`. Two user outages were diagnosable ONLY
from this file, and reaching it meant asking the operator for shell access.
Reach for it whenever freeradius will not start.

get.description:
Why messages are not arriving — the question behind most support mail.

Three things, in one call: how each channel is configured (values through
`_redact()`, so the SMTP password and the WhatsApp access token never leave
the box), what the queue has done in the last 24 h per channel and status,
and the errors themselves. `samm.notif_outbox.last_error` is where a
rejected SMTP login, an expired Meta token or an unlinked WhatsApp number
actually says so, and nothing outside this endpoint could read it.

For the unofficial QR bridge specifically, pair this with
`GET /support/logs?unit=samm-wa-bridge`. Scope: `diagnostics:read`.

Reachability of every service SAMM talks to, from the install's network.

Read-only, and deliberately not a URL fetcher: the targets are the fixed
list above. `ok` means the host ANSWERED — an HTTP 403/405 to a HEAD still
proves the path is open, so read `status` for what it said and `error` for
why nothing came back. `blocked` is the short answer.

All targets are probed in parallel behind one deadline, because the whole
point is that a blocked host does not fail fast: a DNS-black-holed name
stalls per resolved address, so probing seven of them in sequence could
outlast the request itself. Scope: `diagnostics:read`.
get.summary: Can this install reach what SAMM depends on?

get.description:
The three queues that make an install look broken while it is healthy.

A CoA backlog means speed and disconnect changes are not reaching the
routers, so an operator sees "the plan change did nothing". Unapplied
`audit_log` rows mean samm-radius is not draining, so panel actions appear
to be ignored. A webhook backlog means the customer's own integration is
down, not SAMM. Each one is a different owner, and they are indistinguishable
from the panel. (`notif_outbox` has its own endpoint, /support/notifications.)

Same per-status indexed ranges as there, for the same reason. Scope:
`diagnostics:read`.
get.summary: Backlog and failures in every SAMM queue

get.description:
Runs the checks a support engineer would run by hand and returns a
pass/fail per check with a one-line reason.

Unlike /diagnostics — which reports what the install has RECORDED — these
probe the current state: the database answers, the daemons have beaten
recently, every router has been reached, the disk has room, and the AAA
tables are reachable. `ok` is the summary: false means at least one check
failed. Scope: `diagnostics:read`.

post.description:
Restart a single SAMM-owned unit.

The one endpoint in this router that changes the machine, which is why it
needs `services:write` — a scope no support token carries by default. During
the 2026-08 outages the only way to restart a user's FreeRADIUS was to
ask them for a shell; this closes that, without letting a read-only token do
it by accident.

Allow-listed against SAMM's own catalogue: never an arbitrary unit name,
which would make this a systemctl proxy for the whole box. `samm-api` is
handed to the oneshot restart unit because a process cannot restart itself
inside the request that asked for it.

The `systemctl show` / `ls -ld` / `--version` answers, over the API.

Every field here was something support had to obtain by asking the operator
for a shell session during the 2026-08 outages. The unit facts in particular
decide the diagnosis outright: a freeradius unit with an EMPTY
`RuntimeDirectory` cannot recreate /run/freeradius after a reboot, which is
what took two ISPs offline — and it is invisible from every other endpoint.
Read-only, no shell, no secrets. Scope: `diagnostics:read`.

get.description:

An update that fails leaves `update_apply_error` and a stalled

nor was the updater's journal, which is the other half (now
`GET /support/logs?unit=samm-updater`).

`schema_head` against `SAMM_VERSION` is the second question support asks:
an install running new code on an old schema behaves like neither release.
Scope: `diagnostics:read`.

post.description: Register an endpoint. The HMAC signing secret is returned ONCE in this response — store it; deliveries are signed with it (`X-SAMM-Signature`). Unknown event names are ignored; at least one valid event is required. Scope: `webhooks:manage`.

get.description:
The event catalogue, with what each one means.

Subscribing to a name that does not exist is silently useless — the endpoint
is created and simply never fires — so a client that builds its own
subscription list needs to read the catalogue rather than guess it. The
names here are the only values `POST /webhooks` accepts.
get.summary: Every event an endpoint can subscribe to
